title: Planting Trees in the Desert
summary: Why people are planting trees in the desert, which trees they choose, and how they help young trees survive heat and drought.
poll: Planting trees in the desert is worth the hard work.

versions.title: Trees in the Sand
versions.text:
The desert is hot. It is dry. Not many trees grow there. But now, people plant trees in the sand.

Why plant trees? Trees give shade. The air is cool in the shade. Tree roots hold the soil. Then the wind can not blow it away. So there is less dust in the air. Birds can live in the trees, too. And trees make the air clean.

In 2021, Saudi Arabia made a big plan. It will plant ten billion trees! That will take a long time.

Which trees grow best? Trees that have long lived in the desert. The ghaf tree is one. The sidr tree is one, too. They need just a bit of water. Their roots go down deep to find it.

First, each tree starts as a seed. It grows in a pot. A small young tree is a seedling. When it is strong, it goes in the ground.

A thin pipe drips water on its roots. A fence keeps goats and camels out. In a few years, the tree can live on its own.

versions.text:

versions.title: Planting Trees in the Desert
versions.text:
The desert is scorching and dry, and very few trees grow there naturally. Yet today, people are deliberately planting trees in the sand. Why would anyone attempt such a challenging task?

Trees provide shade, and the air beneath them is noticeably cooler. Their roots anchor the soil, which prevents erosion, so the wind cannot carry the soil away and there is less dust. Birds and small animals build shelters among the branches. Trees also absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and release oxygen, which people and animals need to breathe.

In 2021, Saudi Arabia launched the Saudi Green Initiative. Its ambitious goal is to plant ten billion trees across the country over the coming decades.

Which trees grow best? Experts usually select native trees, which have always grown in the region, such as the ghaf, the acacia, and the sidr. These trees can survive drought because their roots extend deep underground to reach hidden water supplies.

Each tree begins as a seed in a nursery, where workers water it and shelter it from the intense sun. When the young tree is sturdy enough, it is transplanted into the ground, usually during the cooler months.

Afterward, a narrow pipe drips water directly onto its roots, and a fence prevents hungry goats and camels from eating it. After a few years, the tree can survive independently.

Planting trees in the desert is far from simple, because rain is rare, summer temperatures can scorch delicate leaves, and some soil contains too much salt. Consequently, many young trees require additional care during their first years, and workers inspect them regularly and replace the ones that die. Saudi Arabia also has laws that punish people who cut down native trees for firewood, because protecting existing trees is as important as planting new ones.

versions.title: Greening the Desert
versions.text:
The desert is scorching and dry, and very few trees grow there naturally, yet people are now deliberately planting trees in the sand. Why would anyone attempt such a challenging task?

Trees provide shade, and the air beneath them is noticeably cooler. Their roots anchor the soil, which prevents erosion, so the wind cannot carry the soil away and dust storms become less severe. The branches shelter birds, insects, and small animals, which increases biodiversity. Trees also absorb carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, and release the oxygen that people and animals need to breathe.

In 2021, Saudi Arabia launched the Saudi Green Initiative, an ambitious plan to plant ten billion trees across the country over the coming decades and to restore large areas of damaged land.

Experts usually select native trees, which have grown in the region for thousands of years, such as the ghaf, the acacia, and the sidr. These species can survive long periods of drought because their roots extend deep underground; the roots of a ghaf tree may reach more than thirty meters down.

Each tree begins as a seed in a nursery, where workers water it and shelter it from the intense sun. When the young tree is sturdy enough, it is transplanted into the ground, usually during the cooler months.

Water is precious, so planters use drip irrigation and sometimes recycled water, which is wastewater that has been cleaned. Fences prevent hungry goats and camels from eating the young trees. After a few years, a tree can usually survive independently.

Planting trees in the desert is far from simple, because rainfall is rare, summer temperatures can scorch delicate leaves, and some soil contains too much salt, so many young trees require extra care during their first years. Saudi Arabia has also introduced laws that punish people who cut down native trees for firewood, since protecting existing trees is just as important as planting new ones. Other countries are attempting similar projects; across Africa, for example, nations are building the Great Green Wall, a belt of trees and plants that is meant to stretch about eight thousand kilometers along the southern edge of the Sahara.

These species can endure prolonged periods of drought because their roots extend deep underground; the roots of a mature ghaf tree may penetrate more than thirty meters below the surface.
